question:
A coding agent proposes splitting a large module into several networked services. Before anyone implements it, how can the team check whether this high-level structure will meet goals that pull against each other, such as response time, hosting cost and ease of future change?

Answer with a list of guidelines. After each guideline, cite the source it comes from: the path of the SWEBOK file if you have it, otherwise a verbatim quote of at least 8 words from the passage, in the form (source: ...).
answer:
The searches are rich and highly convergent. I now have all the SWEBOK passages needed to construct a comprehensive, well-sourced set of guidelines. Here is the answer:

---

## Guidelines for Pre-Implementation Evaluation of a Proposed Multi-Service Architecture

---

### 1. Gather and formalize Architecturally Significant Requirements (ASRs) first

Before evaluating any structural proposal, identify every requirement that influences the architecture — including performance targets, budget constraints, and change-friendliness goals. [SWEBOK excerpt 7355675a3c5d6f7f4b7d]." [SWEBOK excerpt 5e5da7c24168149087a9], and when requirements conflict with constraints, negotiation is used to revise them before design proceeds.

(source: "[SWEBOK excerpt bf2ef9e0191320e52934]'" — /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture Foundations and Design Principles/Software Architecture_ Contexts, Methods, and Design Processes/Architecture Analysis and Synthesis/Architectural Design Analysis and Key Concerns.md)

---

### 2. Explicitly map every stakeholder concern, including cost and evolvability

Architectural concerns span a very wide set including "affordability, agility, … cost, … deployability, … evolvability, … maintainability, modifiability, … performance, … scalability, … sustainability." Each stakeholder group (customers, users, operators, developers) brings different concerns, and an architecture must address not only each concern in isolation but the consequences of their interactions. The team should produce an explicit list of these concerns for the proposed service split before attempting any evaluation.

(source: "[SWEBOK excerpt 7fda26151032383630d5]…" — /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture_ Foundations, Views, and Patterns/Architectural Concerns, Views, and Viewpoints/Stakeholder Concerns in Software Architecture.md)

---

### 3. Apply the Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method (ATAM) to reason about competing quality attributes

The SWEBOK identifies ATAM as the primary structured technique for exactly this situation. "The Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method (ATAM) [SWEBOK excerpt 02150566f2318db6d9d7]." ATAM (along with SAAM and Quality Attribute Workshops) lets the team score the proposed service structure against each goal — response time, cost, modifiability — before writing a line of code.

(source: "The Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method (ATAM) [SWEBOK excerpt eafe65af540d6e472b39]." — /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture Foundations and Design Principles/Evaluating Software Architecture Quality and Fitness/Software Architecture Evaluation and Quality Tradeoffs.md)

---

### 4. Treat quality-attribute trade-offs as the explicit basis for architectural decisions

The SWEBOK warns that quality attributes routinely conflict: "[SWEBOK excerpt b2eae3163f0b2bf88962] easy-to-[SWEBOK excerpt 38d1ec47799c52b25ffe]." Similarly, speed and modifiability pull against each other [SWEBOK excerpt ee1c3543105ac966859b]." The team must surface these tensions for the specific service-split proposal — e.g., will network boundaries add latency that violates the response-time target? — and treat the resulting trade-offs as explicit architectural decisions rather than implicit assumptions.

(source: "[SWEBOK excerpt b2eae3163f0b2bf88962] easy-to-[SWEBOK excerpt 4bdd60ab71ec1b86d925]." — /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture Foundations and Design Principles/Evaluating Software Architecture Quality and Fitness/Software Architecture Evaluation and Quality Tradeoffs.md)

---

### 5. Use multiple architecture views to reason about different quality goals separately

A single diagram cannot simultaneously expose all quality-relevant properties. The SWEBOK recommends separate views for distinct concerns: "[SWEBOK excerpt c86ca47f4d30ff3653e1]." There are also documented viewpoints specifically [SWEBOK excerpt 82af90bc2672255ca8c4]." For the proposed service split, produce at least a component-and-connector view (for latency/response-time reasoning), a deployment view (for hosting cost), and a module view (for modifiability).

(source: "a logical view … a process view … a physical view … a development view … [SWEBOK excerpt 17b4d9b1daf8b8f138bf]." — /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture_ Foundations, Views, and Patterns/Architectural Concerns, Views, and Viewpoints/Architecture Viewpoints and Their Applications.md)

---

### 6. Explicitly analyse distribution-of-components concerns against performance, reliability, and cost

The SWEBOK singles out distribution as a core software-design quality concern: "[SWEBOK excerpt da01806e63341c6e5ab6]." When reviewing the multi-service proposal, the team must ask whether the network boundaries, communication protocols, and hosting topology satisfy all of those properties simultaneously — or whether optimising for one (e.g., fine-grained services for modifiability) degrades another (e.g., latency or hosting cost).

(source: "[SWEBOK excerpt da01806e63341c6e5ab6]." — /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Design Concerns, Documentation, and Modeling/Software Design Concerns and Architectural Patterns.md)

---

### 7. Evaluate architectural "goodness" against four universal questions

The SWEBOK frames architectural goodness as a checklist applicable to any proposal: Is the architecture robust over its lifetime and [SWEBOK excerpt 9ce5245a135792c8c066]? Is it [SWEBOK excerpt 6dc3b00b533e42fac369]? Run the proposed service structure through these four questions, treating each as a formal evaluation criterion before green-lighting implementation.

(source: "[SWEBOK excerpt 85ec64bce62a38642702]?" — /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture Foundations and Design Principles/Evaluating Software Architecture Quality and Fitness/Software Architecture Evaluation and Quality Tradeoffs.md)

---

### 8. Conduct a structured architecture review (not just an informal walkthrough)

The SWEBOK distinguishes informal reviews from structured ones: "[SWEBOK excerpt 2c4b3a63bfe3df0388ac]. [SWEBOK excerpt afba509c3d2b2b2c004f]." For a consequential structural decision such as a module-to-services split, the team should run an active review (where [SWEBOK excerpt aae560b5c3b6a225db0d]) rather than relying on a conversational walkthrough.

(source: "[SWEBOK excerpt 2c4b3a63bfe3df0388ac]." — /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture Foundations and Design Principles/Evaluating Software Architecture Quality and Fitness/Architecture Reviews and Metrics for Quality Assessment.md)

---

### 9. Apply compensatory multi-attribute decision-making to rank the architecture against alternatives

Where several structural variants exist (e.g., coarser vs. finer service granularity), the SWEBOK recommends compensatory multi-criteria techniques: "Compensatory techniques … [SWEBOK excerpt 6ed292052877d4475a99] … [SWEBOK excerpt f94d1f448b7a10788f2a])." ATAM itself is listed as a compensatory multi-attribute technique. Using such a technique lets the team compare "split into N services" vs. "split into M services" on response time, hosting cost, and modifiability in a single quantified comparison.

(source: "[SWEBOK excerpt 672c865fa3278a223282] [SWEBOK excerpt d62e5ade89c458383496]) [SWEBOK excerpt d689423a7aa2ffb6ad23]." — /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Engineering Decision-Making and Financial Analysis/Multi-Criteria Decision-Making and Intangible Assets/Compensatory and Non-Compensatory Decision-Making Techniques.md)

---

### 10. Treat quality-of-service requirements as economic quantities, not binary pass/fail targets

The SWEBOK advises engineers to "[SWEBOK excerpt 408d4ce111dc89e7b1bd]." Response time and modifiability are partly antagonistic; modifiability and reliability are partly complementary. Rather than asking "does the architecture meet the latency budget?" (binary), the team should model value as a function of performance level and find the most cost-effective operating point: "the most cost-effective performance level [is] [SWEBOK excerpt 913045e248677c0dcaf2]." Apply this thinking to response time, hosting spend, and ease of change concurrently.

(source: "[SWEBOK excerpt 097f2541fd1bf8796113] … [SWEBOK excerpt 6f2c53cdbd807e1e876f]." — /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Requirements_ Foundations and Engineering Practices/Requirements Engineering_ Elicitation, Analysis, and Specification/Requirements Engineering_ Viability, Verification, and Stakeholder Management/Performance Thresholds and Cost-Effective Quality Optimization/Cost-Effective Performance and Quality Trade-offs.md)

---

### 11. Compute and monitor architectural metrics for coupling, cohesion, and change-related indicators

Evaluation should not remain purely qualitative. "Various architecture metrics have been defined … [SWEBOK excerpt 2c527c70b741335055ae] … In continuous development paradigms … other metrics have evolved … [SWEBOK excerpt d1ae0d7a64f64379e7b3]." For the proposed service split, calculate inter-service coupling (a proxy for modifiability) and estimate deployment frequency and mean-time-to-restore (proxies for hosting-cost and operational resilience) before committing.

(source: "[SWEBOK excerpt 2c527c70b741335055ae] … [SWEBOK excerpt f1a8636c161cc8bd6768]." — /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture Foundations and Design Principles/Evaluating Software Architecture Quality and Fitness/Software Architecture Metrics and Evaluation.md)

---

### 12. Document every significant architectural decision and its rationale, including rejected alternatives

Decisions made during the pre-implementation review must themselves be recorded. "[SWEBOK excerpt 510e33216e1de5586418]." Undocumented decisions accumulate as architectural technical debt: "[SWEBOK excerpt 5de23d6145b8a2aba5f9]."

(source: "[SWEBOK excerpt 239678aaeb1545ca9a07]." — /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture_ Foundations, Views, and Patterns/Architectural Design Languages, Decisions, and Technical Debt/Documenting Architectural Decisions and Their Rationale.md)

---

### 13. Use simulation or feasibility prototypes to validate dynamic qualities that cannot be observed in a static design

Some qualities (performance, availability) are only observable at runtime and cannot be fully confirmed by static review. The SWEBOK endorses "[SWEBOK excerpt 6eae0b4a568b22a2f8fc])." Before committing to the networked-service structure, run a minimal performance simulation or a narrow spike prototype of the most latency-sensitive service-to-service call to validate response-time assumptions at realistic load levels.

(source: "[SWEBOK excerpt e9370b60de6cf6bb205e])." — /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Design Quality Evaluation and Assessment/Design Analysis and Quality Metrics/Formal Analysis and Dynamic Evaluation Techniques.md)

---

### 14. Use design reviews and inspections of the software design description (SDD) as a formal quality gate

The team's architectural proposal should be crystallised in a Software Design Description (an SDD — "[SWEBOK excerpt ed088e5c1a4f94a914f0]"), and then subjected to formal review. "[SWEBOK excerpt 7a1c84fc7f16c8406a40]." These reviews simultaneously check functional correctness, performance-related structural properties, and long-term modifiability before any implementation begins.

(source: "[SWEBOK excerpt 8b2b5a714c6f8036b811]." — /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Design Quality Evaluation and Assessment/Software Quality Analysis and Evaluation Techniques.md)
